scenes.visual: Title card 'Catching the Brake' over a split image of boreal forest and a coral patch reef (schematic). COLOUR MAP, same in both films: N (population size or density) in WHITE; the per-capita rate and any per-capita line in TEAL; the carrying capacity K as a GOLD dashed line; total growth dN/dt in ORANGE. Dark navy background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Curves are computed from the model with r = 0.2 per day, K = 1,000, N0 = 100 and labelled 'computed'; cartoons and anything not computed are labelled 'schematic'. In this film the fraction of fish dying is a per-capita measure (fraction dying over the study interval), so it is drawn in TEAL; hare densities are WHITE bars.

scenes.tts: The first film tilted the per-capita line by assumption. In a real forest or on a real reef, how would you catch that line tilting?
scenes.visual: A brief recap: the first film's falling TEAL line with the GOLD dashed K marker. A magnifying glass moves over it, then the frame dissolves to a forest.
scenes.narration: The first film tilted the per-capita line by assumption. In a real forest or on a real reef, how would you catch that line tilting?

scenes.tts: Start in the Yukon, near Kloo-ah-nee Lake. Snowshoe hares there rise and fall in a cycle of roughly a decade.
scenes.caption: Start in the Yukon, near Kluane Lake. Snowshoe hares there rise and fall in a cycle of roughly a decade.
scenes.visual: Map pin 'Kluane Lake, Yukon'. A WHITE hare icon over a looping arrow labelled 'cycle of roughly a decade' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Start in the Yukon, near Kluane Lake. Snowshoe hares there rise and fall in a cycle of roughly a decade.

scenes.tts: Charles Krebs and colleagues worked on blocks of forest. They added food, fenced out mammal predators, did both, or did neither.
scenes.caption: Charles Krebs and colleagues worked on blocks of forest. They added food, fenced out mammal predators, did both, or did neither.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two grid of forest squares (reuse the look of the lesson's Kluane figure): 'control', 'food added', 'fenced: mammal predators out', and 'both' outlined in GOLD. A lynx and coyote cartoon sit outside the fence. On-screen: 'blocks about 1 km2', 'eight years'.
scenes.narration: Charles Krebs and colleagues worked on blocks of forest. They added food, fenced out mammal predators, did both, or did neither.

scenes.tts: During the cycle's peak and decline, fencing out mammal predators raised hare density, and so did food. Doing both raised it far more than either alone.
scenes.visual: WHITE bars rise beside each square, relative to control = 1: 'mammal predators out: about 2x', 'food added: about 3x', 'both: about 11x'. Label 'Krebs et al., Science, 1995'.
scenes.narration: During the cycle's peak and decline, fencing out mammal predators raised hare density, and so did food. Doing both raised it far more than either alone.

scenes.tts: So food and predators both limited the hares. But were individuals doing worse at high density? Counts of hares cannot say.
scenes.visual: The bars stay; a caption types out: 'more hares, but are individuals doing worse at high density? These counts cannot say.' A greyed TEAL line with a question mark appears beside the bars.
scenes.narration: So food and predators both limited the hares. But were individuals doing worse at high density? Counts of hares cannot say.

scenes.tts: For that you need a per-capita rate, measured at several densities. Mark Hixon and Mark Carr did this on small patch reefs in the Bahamas.
scenes.visual: Dissolve to small coral patch reefs on sand (schematic). Name card 'Hixon and Carr, Science, 1997'. Map pin 'Lee Stocking Island, Bahamas'.
scenes.narration: For that you need a per-capita rate, measured at several densities. Mark Hixon and Mark Carr did this on small patch reefs in the Bahamas.

scenes.tts: A per-capita measure counts outcomes per individual, not heads. Here it is the fraction of young fish that died during the study on each reef.
scenes.visual: Ten fish icons on one reef; three fade out. A TEAL fraction '3 of 10 = 0.3 died over the study' appears beside them, while a WHITE head count '10 fish' sits greyed out (schematic numbers).
scenes.narration: A per-capita measure counts outcomes per individual, not heads. Here it is the fraction of young fish that died during the study on each reef.

scenes.tts: They stocked newly settled blue kroh-miss, a small reef fish, at different densities. Some reefs got few young fish, some got many.
scenes.caption: They stocked newly settled blue chromis, a small reef fish, at different densities. Some reefs got few young fish, some got many.
scenes.visual: Three reefs with a few, more and many small blue fish cartoons, labelled 'low', 'medium', 'high' starting density.
scenes.narration: They stocked newly settled blue chromis, a small reef fish, at different densities. Some reefs got few young fish, some got many.

scenes.tts: They also crossed two kinds of predator. Residents live on the reef. Transients swim in from open water and move between reefs.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two reef grid (reuse the look of the lesson's Hixon-Carr figure): 'no predators', 'residents only' (a fish in a crevice), 'transients only' (a fish swimming in), 'both' outlined in GOLD.
scenes.narration: They also crossed two kinds of predator. Residents live on the reef. Transients swim in from open water and move between reefs.

scenes.tts: Then they plotted the fraction of young fish that died against starting density. A fraction dying is a per-capita measure, so it is teal.
scenes.visual: Axes: x 'starting density of young chromis', y 'fraction that died' 0 to 1. A TEAL badge on the y axis: 'per-capita measure: fraction dying over the study interval'. No data yet.
scenes.narration: Then they plotted the fraction of young fish that died against starting density. A fraction dying is a per-capita measure, so it is teal.

scenes.tts: With both predator groups present, the line rose steeply. The more young fish that settled on a reef, the larger the share that died.
scenes.visual: For the 'both' treatment, a TEAL line rises steeply from low to high density (schematic, not the paper's data). Label 'both predator groups: rising'.
scenes.narration: With both predator groups present, the line rose steeply. The more young fish that settled on a reef, the larger the share that died.

scenes.tts: That rising line is density-dependent mortality. Predators caused it on these reefs, at least when both kinds hunted there together.
scenes.visual: The rising TEAL line gets a stamp 'density-dependent mortality'. Small resident and transient predator icons sit at its foot, joined by a plus sign.
scenes.narration: That rising line is density-dependent mortality. Predators caused it on these reefs, at least when both kinds hunted there together.

scenes.tts: Now take away one of the two predator groups, either one. Does the teal line still rise as density goes up?
scenes.visual: The GOLD 'both' square dims; the 'residents only' and 'transients only' squares light up. Empty axes wait beside them with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Now take away one of the two predator groups, either one. Does the teal line still rise as density goes up?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown ring; caption 'Predict: with one predator group, does the line still rise?'.

scenes.tts: With only one group, no rise was detected. But one of those tests had low statistical power, too little data to catch a real slope reliably. Not detected is not the same as absent.
scenes.visual: For each one-group treatment, a TEAL line with no detectable slope draws in, with a wide grey band around it (schematic). A tag on one: 'low power'. Caption: 'not detected is not absent'.
scenes.narration: With only one group, no rise was detected. But one of those tests had low statistical power, too little data to catch a real slope reliably. Not detected is not the same as absent.

scenes.tts: Notice what made this a test of density dependence. Not more deaths in total, but a larger fraction of the fish dying.
scenes.visual: Two reefs side by side. Left: few fish, a small number crossed out. Right: many fish, the same fraction crossed out, labelled 'more deaths, same fraction: no tilt'. Then the right reef's crossed-out share grows, labelled 'larger fraction: a tilt'.
scenes.narration: Notice what made this a test of density dependence. Not more deaths in total, but a larger fraction of the fish dying.

scenes.tts: The hares and the kroh-miss answer two different questions. Adding food and removing predators showed what limited the hares. The kroh-miss showed density dependence, within one generation and across reefs.
scenes.caption: The hares and the chromis answer two different questions. Adding food and removing predators showed what limited the hares. The chromis showed density dependence, within one generation and across reefs.
scenes.visual: Left: the WHITE Kluane bars, labelled 'treatments vs control: what limits'. Right: the rising TEAL reef line, labelled 'per-capita deaths: density dependence (one generation, across reefs)'.
scenes.narration: The hares and the chromis answer two different questions. Adding food and removing predators showed what limited the hares. The chromis showed density dependence, within one generation and across reefs.

scenes.tts: A brake is negative density dependence. As density rises, deaths rise or births fall, so net per-capita growth falls. You find it only by measuring per-capita rates.
scenes.visual: The rising TEAL death-fraction line from the two-predator reefs, labelled 'death part of the net rate', slides beside the first film's falling TEAL net per-capita growth line. Both are labelled 'per-capita, changing with density'; a GOLD bracket over the falling line reads 'negative density dependence: a brake'.
scenes.narration: A brake is negative density dependence. As density rises, deaths rise or births fall, so net per-capita growth falls. You find it only by measuring per-capita rates.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'A brake makes net per-capita growth fall as density rises.'
